entry: City in [[Northern Ireland]], on both banks of the River Foyle. Officially Londonderry, Derry is the second-largest city in Northern Ireland after [[Belfast]], with 85,279 residents in the 2021 census. The name derives from the Irish *Daire* or *Doire*, meaning "oak-grove." It was changed to Londonderry in 1613 during the Plantation of [[Ulster]]. A royal charter of April 10, 1662, confirmed the official name, which a High Court decision reaffirmed in 2007. Derry was the first UK City of Culture, in 2013.

Capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of [[Iowa]]. Named after the Des Moines River, a name likely derived from the French for "River of the Monks." The city was incorporated in 1851 as Fort Des Moines and shortened to Des Moines in 1857. Its population was 214,133 at the 2020 census. It is the county seat of Polk County and a major center of the U.S. insurance industry. As the state capital, Des Moines hosts the first caucuses of the presidential primary cycle, and many presidential candidates set up campaign headquarters there.

Artificial process converting salt water, generally seawater, to fresh water for human consumption or irrigation. Along with recycled wastewater, desalination is one of the few water resources independent of rainfall, but it is generally more costly than surface water, groundwater or water recycling because of its energy use. Processes are thermal, as in [[Distillation|distillation]], or membrane-based, as in [[Reverse osmosis|reverse osmosis]], and both produce [[Brine|brine]] as a by-product. [[Aristotle]] observed that evaporated seawater condenses as fresh water, but large-scale desalination became feasible only in the modern period. As of 2020, global capacity was roughly 97 million m³/day from over 16,800 operating plants. In 2018 the energy intensity of desalination was about 3 kWh/m³, improved by a factor of 10 from 20–30 kWh/m³ in 1970.

Arid climate subtype with a severe excess of evaporation over precipitation. The [[Köppen climate classification|Köppen]] system divides it into hot (BWh) and cold (BWk) variants, separated by a mean annual temperature of 18 °C. The hot desert climate is the most extensive Köppen type, covering about 14.2% of Earth's land area. Most desert climates receive 25–200 mm of rainfall a year. In the [[Atacama Desert]] of northern [[Chile]], average rainfall over 17 years was only 5 mm, while Death Valley in the United States reports 60 mm annually.

Abandonment of military duty or post without permission, with the intention of not returning. It contrasts with temporary unauthorized absence, or absence without leave (AWOL). The U.S. Army, British Armed Forces and Canadian Armed Forces call absence without a valid pass, liberty or leave AWOL, but the [[United States Marine Corps]], Navy and Coast Guard generally use the term unauthorized absence. Personnel are dropped from unit rolls after thirty days and then listed as deserters, yet under U.S. military law desertion depends on a determined intent not to return, not on time away. During [[World War I]], the Australian government refused to allow members of the First Australian Imperial Force to be executed for desertion, despite British pressure. In 2011, [[Vienna]] decided to honor Austrian [[Wehrmacht]] deserters.

Cuban-American actor, bandleader and television producer. Born in Santiago de Cuba, Arnaz fled with his family to Miami after the Cuban Revolution of 1933. He played Ricky Ricardo in the sitcom *I Love Lucy* opposite his wife, [[Lucille Ball]]. Arnaz and Ball are credited with pioneering the syndicated rerun, and they co-founded Desilu Productions. Arnaz later produced series including *The Untouchables*. He was known for playing the conga drums and popularized the conga line in the United States.

Construction of procedures for [[Experiment|experiments]] that attempt to explain how changes in one aspect of a system affect others. Designers decide which aspects of a system to change and which to control, based on hypotheses about sources of variance. A design selects independent, dependent and control variables and plans the experiment under statistically optimal conditions within available resources. Main concerns include validity, reliability, replicability and statistical power. Randomization, replication and blocking are basic principles, and the method is a key tool in Quality by Design (QbD) frameworks. Results are often analyzed with [[Analysis of variance|analysis of variance]]. Sequential experiments, in which each design may depend on earlier results, form the field of sequential analysis, pioneered by Abraham Wald.

South African Anglican bishop and anti-apartheid activist. Tutu was the first black African to serve as Bishop of Johannesburg (1985–86) and then Archbishop of [[Cape Town]] (1986–96). Theologically, he sought to fuse black theology with African theology. As general secretary of the South African Council of Churches from 1978 to 1985, he emphasized non-violent protest and foreign economic pressure against apartheid. After the 1994 election, [[Nelson Mandela]] selected him to chair the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which investigated human rights abuses by both pro- and anti-apartheid groups. Tutu later campaigned for gay rights and opposed the Iraq War. He won the Nobel Peace Prize. Many white South Africans considered him too radical, while Jewish groups accused him of making [[Antisemitism|antisemitic]] statements.

American primetime television [[Soap opera|soap opera]] (2004–2012). Created by Marc Cherry, it ran for eight seasons and 180 episodes on ABC, set on Wisteria Lane in the fictional town of Fairview. The story is told through the eyes of a friend and neighbor who takes her own life in the pilot, and the series explores the secrets and crimes behind a suburban neighborhood's perfect facades. The ensemble included Teri Hatcher, Felicity Huffman, Marcia Cross and [[Eva Longoria]]. Its first five seasons ranked among the top ten most-watched series, and it won multiple Primetime Emmy, Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild Awards.

Sweet food served at the end of a meal, such as [[Cake|cake]], [[Biscuit|biscuit]] or [[Ice cream|ice cream]]. The term comes from the French *desservir*, "to clear the table," and originally referred to the final course of a meal. Historically the dessert course drew on foods "from the storeroom," including fresh, dried and stewed fruit, nuts, cheese, dry biscuits and ices. Sweet kitchen dishes such as pastries and custards were served as a separate course, and by the 20th century sweet entremets had come to be included among desserts. Sugar remained rare in Europe until the [[Crusades]] and later colonization spread its use. The word is most used in Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand and the [[United States]], while the [[United Kingdom]] uses "pudding," "sweets" or "afters."

American girl group formed in [[Houston]], Texas, in 1990. Its principal members were [[Beyoncé]], Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams. Signed to [[Columbia Records]] in 1996, the group released the best-selling album *The Writing's on the Wall* (1999), which produced the US number-one singles "Bills, Bills, Bills" and "Say My Name." *Survivor* (2001) yielded the US number-one singles "Independent Women" and "Bootylicious." The group disbanded in 2006, but its members have reunited several times. Its accolades include three [[Grammy Awards]] and a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Fast, maneuverable [[Warship|warship]] built to escort larger vessels and defend them against a wide range of threats. Destroyers were conceived in the late 19th century as a defense against [[Torpedo|torpedo]] boats, and by [[World War I]] most navies had shortened the term "torpedo boat destroyer" to "destroyer." After [[World War II]] they grew from 2,200 tons (Allen M. Sumner class) to as much as 9,600 tons (Arleigh Burke class, from 1991). Guided missiles let destroyers take over roles once held by battleships and cruisers. Since the late 20th century they have been the global standard for surface combatants, and Arleigh Burke-class ships carry more than 90 missiles.

Subtype of [[Crime|crime]] and mystery fiction in which an investigator, professional, amateur or retired, solves a crime, often a [[Murder|murder]]. The genre began in the mid-19th century and remains popular, especially in novels. Famous heroes include C. Auguste Dupin, [[Sherlock Holmes]], Miss Marple and Hercule Poirot. [[Arthur Conan Doyle]]'s Sherlock Holmes stories, beginning with *A Study in Scarlet* (1887), popularized the eccentric genius detective. The oldest known example is "The Three Apples" from [[One Thousand and One Nights]], in which a vizier must solve a murder under threat of execution, and the caliph [[Harun al-Rashid]] appears in it. British Golden Age fiction, including [[Agatha Christie]]'s Poirot and Marple novels, produced fair-play puzzles, while American hard-boiled fiction, including the novels of [[Raymond Chandler]], focused on gritty urban settings.

Cleaning product whose main functional components are surfactants. Surfactants have a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail, reduce [[Surface tension|surface tension]], and form micelles that lift grease and soil from surfaces. Detergents often include water, builders to soften water, [[Enzyme|enzymes]] that break down proteins, fats or starches, and dyes or fragrances. The word derives from the [[Latin]] *detergere*, "to wipe off." Conventionally, the term refers to synthetic compounds rather than [[Soap|soap]], which is a salt of natural fatty acids. Alkylbenzene sulfonates are more soluble than soap in hard water. Synthetic detergents were first developed commercially in Germany during [[World War I]] to replace fats needed for soap. Phosphate builders contributed to eutrophication, and many regions have phased them out since the 1970s.

Scalar value computed from the entries of a square [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]. A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero, and the determinant of a product of matrices is the product of their determinants. For real linear transformations, the determinant gives the factor by which volume changes, and its sign shows whether orientation is preserved. Determinants can be computed efficiently by [[Gaussian elimination]], and Cramer's rule expresses the solutions of linear systems in terms of determinants. The concept emerged in the late 17th century with [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], who studied values associated with arrays of numbers for solving equations. The characteristic polynomial, whose roots are the eigenvalues of a matrix, is defined as a determinant.

Metaphysical view that all events in the [[Universe|universe]] can occur only in one possible way. Determinism is often contrasted with [[Free will|free will]], although some philosophers argue that the two are compatible. Causal determinism holds that every event results from preceding events and the laws of nature. The antonym is indeterminism, the view that events are not deterministically caused. The idea appears in ancient Western thought and in Eastern philosophy, including the doctrine of [[Karma|karma]]. In 1814 [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] described a hypothetical intellect that could compute the whole course of the cosmos from a complete snapshot of its particles and forces. Quantum mechanics has been interpreted both as introducing fundamental indeterminism and in deterministic ways, while [[Chaos theory|chaos theory]] complicates prediction without denying causality.

Most populous city in the U.S. state of [[Michigan]]. Founded in 1701 by French explorers as Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit, the city became an industrial hub in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its population peaked at 1.85 million at the 1950 census and has since declined by more than 65 percent. Detroit is the center of the U.S. [[Automotive industry|automotive industry]], and General Motors, Ford and Stellantis are headquartered in Metro Detroit. The city gave rise to [[Motown]] and techno and contributed to jazz, hip-hop, rock and punk. In 2013 Detroit became the largest U.S. city to file for bankruptcy, and it exited in 2014. In 2015 [[UNESCO]] named it a "City of Design," the first U.S. city so designated. The 2020 census counted 639,111 residents.

Stable [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] isotope with one neutron, also called heavy hydrogen. Its name comes from the Greek *deuteros*, "second." American chemist [[Harold Urey]] discovered it in 1931, and the discovery won him a Nobel Prize in 1934. Nearly all deuterium found in nature was synthesized in the [[Big Bang]] 13.8 billion years ago. Deuterium is used in most [[Thermonuclear weapon|thermonuclear weapons]], in many fusion power experiments, and as the most effective neutron moderator, primarily in [[Heavy water|heavy water]] reactors. It is also an isotopic label in biogeochemistry and NMR spectroscopy.

German state-funded international broadcaster, broadcasting since 1953. Headquartered in [[Bonn]], with television produced mainly in [[Berlin]], it offers satellite channels in English, Spanish, [[Arabic]] and Russian. Its work is regulated by the Deutsche Welle Act, which states that content is intended to be independent of German government influence; debate has centered on whether state funding affects that independence. Chancellor [[Konrad Adenauer]] supported its creation. It sees itself in the tradition of the first German foreign broadcaster of the [[Weimar Republic]].

Indic script used in the [[Indian subcontinent]]. A left-to-right abugida based on the ancient Brahmi script, it was in regular use by the 8th century CE and reached its modern form by 1000 CE. It is one of the official scripts of [[India]] and [[Nepal]]. Its 48 primary characters include 14 vowels and 34 consonants, and it is the fourth most widely adopted writing system in the world, used for over 120 languages, the most popular of which is [[Hindi]]. The script has no letter case and is recognized by a horizontal line along the top of full letters. It writes [[Sanskrit]] and [[Pali|Pāḷi]], and it is closely related to the Nandinagari script of ancient South Indian manuscripts.

Country with a high quality of life, developed economy and advanced technological infrastructure. Criteria include [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]] (GDP), per capita income, industrialization and infrastructure, and which countries qualify is debated. The [[Human Development Index]] ranks countries by life expectancy, education and income. Definitions differ among the [[United Nations]], the World Bank and the [[International Monetary Fund]]. As of 2023, advanced economies made up 57.3% of global GDP at nominal value and 41.1% at [[Purchasing power parity|purchasing power parity]] (PPP), according to the IMF. The UN Statistics Division describes the designations as intended for statistical convenience.

Process of growth to maturity, beginning with fertilization. When a [[Sperm|sperm]] cell penetrates an egg released from the [[Ovary|ovary]], the resulting zygote is diploid, with 46 [[Chromosome|chromosomes]]. The zygote develops into an [[Embryo|embryo]] that implants in the [[Uterus|uterus]], and the germinal stage ends at about 10 days of gestation. The embryo becomes a [[Fetus|fetus]] about eight weeks after fertilization. Growth continues after birth through childhood and [[Adolescence|adolescence]] into [[Adult|adulthood]], shaped by genetic, hormonal and environmental factors.

Scientific study of how [[Animal|animals]] and [[Plant|plants]] grow and develop. The field also studies regeneration, [[Asexual reproduction|asexual reproduction]], [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]], and the growth and differentiation of [[Stem cell|stem cells]] within adult organisms. Embryonic development of animals involves tissue patterning, tissue growth and morphogenesis, which creates the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Cell differentiation forms functional cell types such as nerve, muscle and liver cells. Plant cells are mostly immotile, so plant morphogenesis proceeds through differential growth rather than cell movement.

Scientific study of how and why the human mind grows and changes over a lifetime. Originally concerned with [[Infant|infants]] and children, the field now covers adolescence, adulthood and aging. It examines physical, cognitive and social-emotional development, and debates nature and nurture as well as stages versus dynamic systems of development. [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] and [[John B. Watson]] are typically cited as its foundations. [[Sigmund Freud]] proposed psychosexual stages, and [[Erik Erikson]] described eight phases of psychosocial development, each with its own developmental crisis. [[Jean Piaget]] described four stages of cognitive development, and [[Lev Vygotsky]] emphasized social interaction in cognitive growth.

Behavior that violates [[Social norm|social norms]], from formal rules such as [[Crime|crime]] to informal violations of folkways and mores. Deviance is relative to place and time: killing is generally considered wrong, but governments may permit it in warfare or self-defense. A [[Taboo|taboo]] is a strong social prohibition, such as [[Murder|murder]], rape or incest, that exists in most societies. [[Émile Durkheim]] argued that deviance is a normal part of social organization, because it affirms cultural values and defines moral boundaries. Robert Merton's strain theory attributes deviance to mismatches between culturally prescribed goals and legitimate means of reaching them. Howard Becker's labeling theory holds that deviance depends on the labels others apply to behavior.
